title: Structs and methods
summary: Group fields into one named type, then give that type its own methods.

blocks.html: Related values want to travel together. A player has a name and a score; keeping them in two loose variables means every function takes two parameters and nothing stops you from pairing the wrong ones. A struct groups them into a single named type with named fields.

blocks.title: declare, build, mutate

blocks.html:
A field is reached with a dot: p.score, read or written. Writing needs the binding to be mut — let mut p, not let p — because mut is a property of the binding, not of the struct type. The field list order in the literal does not have to match the declaration.

Ownership applies field by field. The name field is a String, so Player owns that string and drops it with itself when p leaves the scope.

blocks.title: shorthand and update syntax

blocks.html: Two shortcuts to read carefully. If a local variable has the same name as the field, writing just title means title: title — that is the field init shorthand. And ..a fills any field you did not name from a, so width is overridden while height and title are taken from a. Taken, not copied: those fields move out of a, so a String field leaves a partly moved and unusable as a whole afterwards.

blocks.title: inside a Player value
blocks.ascii:
stack                        heap
   p     +----------------+
         | name   ptr ----|-----> "ada"
         |        len   3 |
         |        cap   3 |
         | score       10 |
         +----------------+

   One value with two named fields. The name
   field carries its own pointer, so Player
   owns heap memory through it.

blocks.title: a tuple struct

blocks.html: When the field names would be noise, drop them. A tuple struct keeps the same one-type grouping but reaches its fields by position: p.0, p.1. It is a distinct type — Point(3, 4) and a plain (3, 4) are not interchangeable — which is the point: a Meters(u32) will not accept a Feet(u32).

blocks.title: impl: associated function and methods

blocks.html:
An impl block attaches functions to the type. Inside it, self is the value you were called on, and the sigil in front of it is a borrow from the last chapter: &self reads without taking ownership, &mut self changes the value in place. So c.bump() is sugar for Counter::bump(&mut c), which is why c has to be mut.

No self at all means an associated function: it belongs to the type, not to an instance. fn new() -> Self returns a fresh value, and we call it as Counter::new() using ::. That is a convention, not a keyword — nothing forces the name new.

blocks.title: printing a struct

blocks.html: println!("{}", p) will not compile for a struct: there is no built-in way to print an arbitrary type. {:?} asks for the debug format instead, which is only available if the type implements Debug — and #[derive(Debug)] above the struct makes the compiler write that implementation for you. {:#?} is the same thing pretty-printed one field per line, which is what you want on a large struct. Printing structs in a custom format is a job for a trait, and traits arrive in chapter 13.

quiz.q: Which change makes the line p.score = 25; compile?
quiz.why: mut belongs on the binding. A struct's fields can only be written through a mut binding, even if the struct type itself is unchanged.

quiz.q: What does &self in a method signature mean?
options: The method borrows the value instead of taking ownership
The method returns a reference to itself
The method is allowed to modify the value
quiz.why: &self is a shared borrow, so calling the method leaves the caller's value intact. Modifying needs &mut self.

quiz.q: How do you call fn new() -> Self when it is defined in impl Player?
quiz.why: With no self parameter it is an associated function, so it is called on the type with the double colon, not on an instance.

exercise.brief: Define a struct Song with a title: String and a plays: u32. In an impl block give it fn new(title: String) -> Self that starts plays at 0, and fn play(&mut self) that adds one play. In main, create "echo", play it twice, then print one line holding the title, the word played, the count, and times, for example: echo played 2 times
exercise.hint: fn new(title: String) -> Self { Song { title, plays: 0 } } uses the field init shorthand. play needs &mut self so it can do self.plays += 1. In main the binding must be mutable: let mut song = Song::new(String::from("echo"));
